<user_query>
soft link vs hard link?
</user_query>

A **hard link** and a **soft link** (symbolic link) are both ways to refer to a file, but they work very differently.

## Hard link

A hard link is another **directory entry that points to the same inode** (same data on disk).

- Multiple filenames can refer to **one actual file**.
- All hard links are **peers** - there is no "original" vs "link".
- Deleting one name does not delete the data until **all** hard links are gone.
- Cannot cross filesystems (inode must exist on the same volume).
- Usually **cannot** link directories (except by root on some systems).
- If you move/rename one hard link, the others still work.

Example:

```bash
ln file.txt hardlink.txt
```

Both names are the same file.

## Soft link (symbolic link)

A soft link is a **small file that stores a path** to another file or directory.

- It is its own file with its own inode.
- It points **by path**, not directly to data.
- If the target is deleted or moved, the symlink becomes **broken**.
- Can point across filesystems.
- Can link to directories.
- Can point to non-existent paths (useful for some setups).

Example:

```bash
ln -s /path/to/file.txt symlink.txt
```

`symlink.txt` is a pointer; `file.txt` is the target.

## Quick comparison

| | Hard link | Soft link |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Another name for same file | A file containing a path |
| Target deleted | Data remains (other links still work) | Link breaks |
| Cross filesystem | No | Yes |
| Link to directory | Usually no | Yes |
| Followed by default | Yes (it *is* the file) | Yes (`cat symlink` reads target) |

## Mental model

- **Hard link**: two door labels on the same room.
- **Soft link**: a sign on the wall saying "the room is down that hallway".

## Common uses

- **Soft links**: `~/bin` -> actual install dir, versioned tool paths, `.env` pointing elsewhere, macOS `/tmp` style indirection.
- **Hard links**: deduplication/backups (same bytes, one copy), some build systems, preserving data when one path is removed but another remains.

On macOS/Linux, `ls -l` shows symlinks with `->`. Hard links look like normal files; use `ls -li` and compare **inode numbers** to see if two names share the same file.

content.text:
Two things were blocking you:

## Root cause

Your `.tmux.conf` had `mode-keys vi`, but the **running tmux server never loaded it** - it was still on `mode-keys emacs`. In emacs copy mode, `j`/`k` and `Ctrl-U`/`Ctrl-D` are not bound for scrolling.

I reloaded the config; it now shows `mode-keys vi`.

## How to navigate

| Keys | What they do |
|------|--------------|
| `Ctrl-b` then `[` | Enter copy mode (scrollback) |
| `j` / `k` | Line down / up (in copy mode) |
| `Ctrl-U` / `Ctrl-D` | Half page up / down |
| `q` or `Esc` | Exit copy mode |

**`Ctrl-U` / `Ctrl-D` now also work without prefix** - tmux catches them before zsh. Tradeoff: they no longer kill-to-start-of-line / EOF in the shell while inside tmux.

**`j` / `k` only work in copy mode** (after `Ctrl-b [`). Binding them globally would stop you typing those letters in the shell.

## Try it now

Inside tmux:

1. `Ctrl-b` `[` - enter copy mode (status bar should say `[copy]`)
2. `j` / `k` or `Ctrl-U` / `Ctrl-D` - scroll
3. `q` - exit

Or skip step 1 and just use `Ctrl-U` / `Ctrl-D` directly.

## If it still fails

Restart the tmux server so all sessions pick up the config:

```bash
tmux kill-server   # kills all sessions
tmux new -s main
```

Or reload manually anytime:

```bash
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf
```

<user_query>
how to undo last git commit (keep worktree unchanged)
</user_query>

To undo the last commit but **keep all your file changes**, use `git reset`:

## Keep changes staged (most common)

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```

- Removes the last commit
- Files stay exactly as they were in that commit
- Changes remain **staged** (`git add` state)

## Keep changes but unstage them

```bash
git reset HEAD~1
```

Same as `--mixed` (the default):

- Removes the last commit
- Files stay modified in your working tree
- Changes are **unstaged**

## Quick comparison

| Command | Commit removed? | Working tree | Staging area |
|---------|-----------------|--------------|--------------|
| `git reset --soft HEAD~1` | Yes | Unchanged | Staged |
| `git reset HEAD~1` | Yes | Unchanged | Unstaged |
| `git reset --hard HEAD~1` | Yes | **Discarded** | **Discarded** |

Avoid `--hard` if you want to keep your work.

## If you already pushed

Resetting rewrites local history. After reset, you'd need:

```bash
git push --force-with-lease
```

Only do that if you're sure no one else depends on that commit.

## Alternative: keep history, revert the commit

If the commit is already shared and you don't want to rewrite history:

```bash
git revert HEAD
```

That creates a **new** commit that undoes the last one, instead of removing it.

**For your case** ("keep worktree unchanged"): use `git reset --soft HEAD~1` if you want to recommit, or `git reset HEAD~1` if you want the changes unstaged.

<timestamp>Sunday, Aug 30, 2026, 5:53 PM (UTC+8)</timestamp>
<user_query>
if i restart tmux, shouldn't it reload the tmux conf?
</user_query>

Yes - but only when the **tmux server** actually restarts, not just when you detach/reattach.

## When config reloads automatically

Tmux reads `~/.tmux.conf` when the **server starts**:

```bash
tmux kill-server    # stop the server
tmux new -s main      # new server -> reads ~/.tmux.conf
```

Also if you exit **all** sessions (last pane/window closes), the server dies. The next `tmux new` loads config fresh.

## When it does NOT reload

| Action | Config reloaded? |
|--------|------------------|
| `tmux detach` / `tmux attach` | No - same server |
| Open a new window/tab in existing server | No |
| Close one terminal, server still has other sessions | No |

Those keep the **old** config in memory until you `source-file` or kill the server.

## Why yours didn't work before

Your server was already running with `mode-keys emacs`. You had `mode-keys vi` in `.tmux.conf`, but that file is only applied at server start (unless you run `source-file`).

So:

- **Restart server** (`kill-server` then `new`) = reloads config
- **Just reattach** = does not

If you want to apply changes without killing sessions:

```bash
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf
```

<timestamp>Sunday, Aug 30, 2026, 5:54 PM (UTC+8)</timestamp>
<user_query>
does killing the server kills all sections
</user_query>

Yes. `tmux kill-server` stops the entire tmux **server**, which kills **all sessions**, **all windows**, and **all panes**.

Anything running inside them (editors, servers, long jobs) is terminated unless it was started detached from tmux (e.g. with `nohup` or `disown`).

## Safer alternatives

If you only want to reload config without losing sessions:

```bash
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf
```

If you want to kill **one** session:

```bash
tmux kill-session -t session-name
```

List sessions first:

```bash
tmux ls
```

## Summary

| Command | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| `tmux kill-server` | Kills **everything** |
| `tmux kill-session -t 5` | Kills only session `5` |
| `exit` in last pane | Closes that session (server dies if it was the last one) |

how do i add an origin to my repo?
</user_query>

To add a remote named `origin`:

```bash
git remote add origin <repository-url>
```

Examples:

```bash
# HTTPS
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git

# SSH
git remote add origin git@github.com:username/repo.git
```

Verify:

```bash
git remote -v
```

## First push

If the branch has no upstream yet:

```bash
git push -u origin main
```

Use your actual branch name if it is not `main` (e.g. `master`).

## If `origin` already exists

Change the URL instead of adding:

```bash
git remote set-url origin <new-url>
```

## Check current remotes

```bash
git remote -v
```

<user_query>
what's the difference between -m and -M in git branch? any diff?
</user_query>

`-m` and `-M` both **rename/move a branch**. The only difference is what happens if the **new name already exists**.

## `-m` (move, safe)

```bash
git branch -m old-name new-name
```

- Renames the branch
- **Fails** if `new-name` already exists

## `-M` (move, force)

```bash
git branch -M old-name new-name
```

- Renames the branch
- **Overwrites** `new-name` if it already exists

Same pattern as:

| Safe | Force |
|------|-------|
| `-d` delete branch | `-D` force delete |
| `-m` rename branch | `-M` force rename |

## Common usage

Rename the **current** branch (no old name needed):

```bash
git branch -m new-name
```

Force-rename current branch to `main` (common when init created `master`):

```bash
git branch -M main
```

That `-M main` is popular because it renames to `main` even if a `main` branch already exists.

**Short answer:** `-m` = rename unless name taken; `-M` = rename and overwrite if taken.
